verses.translation_literal: To the choirmaster: 'Do not destroy.' Of David. A miktam. When he fled from before Saul in the cave.
verses.translation_dramatic: For the choirmaster, to the tune that begins 'Do not destroy.' A song of David, a miktam, from the hour when he ran from Saul's face and went to ground in the cave.
verses.directors_commentary:
A superscription is stage direction, and this one is full of it. 'To the choirmaster' means the song was handed to the temple musicians for performance. 'Do not destroy' (al-tashchet) is most likely the name of a tune or the opening words of a melody, and the same cry heads Psalms 58, 59 and 75; Rashi and Meiri hear it as David's own prayer, 'Do not destroy me, LORD.' 'Miktam' also heads Psalm 16 and Psalms 56 to 60; its meaning is lost, and KJV's 'Michtam' is simply a transliteration. Play it as a technical term the first audience knew and we do not.

The last clause is the historical frame: 'when he fled from before Saul in the cave.' KJV puts all this outside the psalm as an unnumbered heading, so its verse 1 is our verse 2; the Hebrew counts the title as verse 1. 'From before' (mipnei) is literal: David runs out of Saul's sight, as a hunted man flees a face. The tradition reads the cave of 1 Samuel 24 (Radak, Meiri), where David and his men sit deep inside as Saul enters.

philological_notes.note: 'Do not destroy', from shachat, to ruin or corrupt. Meiri links the verb to David's words to Abishai over the sleeping Saul, 'Do not destroy him' (1 Sam 26:9), so the title may hint at the very restraint the psalm tells.
A psalm-type label of uncertain meaning; older guesses connect it with ketem, 'gold', hence 'a golden/treasured poem' (YLT: 'a secret treasure'), but this is a conjecture.

verses.translation_literal: Be gracious to me, O God, be gracious to me, for in you my soul has taken refuge, and in the shadow of your wings I will take refuge until the destructions pass by.
verses.translation_dramatic: Be gracious to me, God. Be gracious to me. My whole self has run to you for cover, and under the shadow of your wings I will stay, hidden, until the ruin has gone over and past.
verses.directors_commentary:
The doubled 'be gracious to me' is a cry, not a figure of speech; Radak and Metzudat David say a man in terror repeats himself, and Malbim hears two requests, one for grace not to strike Saul, one for grace not to be struck. Say each 'be gracious' at a different pitch.

Two images of shelter. 'Take refuge' (chasah) is the verb for fleeing to a place that can hold you, rock, cave, tent, and the verse uses it twice, first as a done deed (the perfect), then as a promise (the imperfect): 'has taken refuge ... will take refuge.' KJV's 'trusteth' and 'make my refuge' flatten the repetition into two different verbs. The 'shadow of your wings' is the bird covering its young, but it also echoes the winged cherubim over the ark in the sanctuary; the man is in a cave and asks for a cover that no cave gives.

'Destructions' (havot) is plural, an intensive: the engulfing calamity, a storm-front that must 'pass by', the verb used of a flood or a tempest crossing a land. KJV's 'calamities be overpast' is faithful; its 'these' is not in the Hebrew. Radak and Rashi read it as the evil Saul plans, which will pass.

philological_notes.note: From chanan, to show unmerited favour; it is the plea of the weaker party who has no claim. The doubling intensifies it.
A rare form, perfect with a final yod where one expects he; Radak says the yod stands for the he, for ease of reading. The verb is 'to flee for shelter'.
Plural noun of havvah, 'ruin, destruction, engulfing disaster'; Metzudat Zion glosses it 'breaking' (sheber), Radak 'a shattering and an evil matter'.

verses.translation_literal: I will call to God Most High, to the God who completes [it] for me.
verses.translation_dramatic: I will call out to God Most High, to the God who finishes what he has begun for me.
verses.directors_commentary:
Two titles for God, one over the other, as when a petitioner climbs through a palace calling the ranks. 'Elyon', 'Most High', is the title that places him above every power in the room, and Ibn Ezra notes the point of it: the man calling is at the lowest place on earth, in a cave. 'God who completes' (el gomer) has no object, and that gap is the verse. KJV fills it with 'performeth all things', which is its own gloss; Hebrew gamar means to bring to an end, to finish. Radak and Meiri supply 'the kingdom': God will complete what he began when David was anointed, and Metzudat David reads it as 'what he promised'.

The verb is the imperfect 'I will call', a vow and a present act at once. Play it quietly. The voice is calm because it has chosen whom to address.

philological_notes.note: 'Most High', an old title of God as supreme over other gods (Gen 14:18-20); in the mouth of a man in a hole it is deliberately a statement of height.

'one who completes on my behalf'; the verb has no stated object. Radak and Meiri read it as completing the kingship promised to David; the same verb gamar appears in Psalm 138:8 'The LORD will complete for me'.

verses.translation_literal: He will send from heaven and he will save me; he has reproached the one who gasps after me. Selah. God will send his covenant loyalty and his faithfulness.
verses.translation_dramatic: He will send down from heaven and save me; he has shamed the one who pants at my heels. Selah. God will send out his steadfast love and his truth.
verses.directors_commentary:
The structure is a refrain, 'he will send ... God will send', and the two sends carry different cargo: the first is rescue from heaven, the second is two personified attendants, chesed and emet, covenant loyalty and faithfulness, dispatched like messengers. KJV's 'mercy and truth' is warmer than the words; chesed is loyalty held to a pledge, and the pledge is the kingship promised to David. Metzudat David says emet is the truth of that promise.

The middle clause is the puzzle: the verb 'reproached' (cheref) is a perfect, and its subject is not marked. Meiri reads it as a prophetic past with God as subject: the enemy is already shamed and brought low. Radak reads the pursuer as the one who reproached: Saul would not be chasing David had he not despised the word of the LORD, for he knew that Samuel had anointed David on God's command. KJV ('the reproach of him that would swallow me up'), YLT and ASV likewise make the pursuer the one who reproaches, so the line becomes a taunt, and Malbim hears that taunt as sarcasm: the enemies sneer 'let him send from heaven and save him', and David takes their joke as creed. KJV's noun phrase also blurs the verb into a noun and smooths over the grammar.

Shoafi: KJV 'swallow up' follows Rashi and Metzudat Zion, who gloss it as swallowing; the root sha'af is a gasp or gulp, hence a predator panting for its prey, the picture of a wolf at his heels. Selah, falling mid-verse, is a musical pause: the instruments hold, and the singer starts again on the second 'he will send'.

philological_notes.note: Piel perfect, 'he reproached, taunted'. Who the subject is divides the readers: Meiri takes God as subject in a prophetic past, so the enemy is shamed; Radak takes Saul as the one who has despised God's word; Malbim takes the enemies as mockers.
Participle 'one who pants/gasps after', also 'tramples' in other uses (Amos 2:7); Rashi glosses it as the one who says he will swallow me, Metzudat Zion as 'swallowing'.
The pair 'covenant loyalty and faithfulness' is a standard formula for God's character (Exod 34:6). Here they are 'sent', almost as envoys.

token_glosses.gloss: the one who gasps after me

verses.translation_literal: My soul is in the midst of lions; I lie down [among] blazing ones, sons of man, their teeth a spear and arrows, and their tongue a sharp sword.
verses.translation_dramatic: My soul is in the middle of lions. I lie down among men who burn, sons of Adam: their teeth are spear and arrows, and their tongue a whetted sword.
verses.directors_commentary:
Here the psalm tilts into nightmare. The scene is a bed made in the lions' den, and the shock is in the last word: they are not beasts, they are 'sons of man'. Malbim's observation is the sharp one: lions have teeth of bone, these have teeth of iron, spears and arrows; fire-breathing serpents have venom, these have a tongue that is a sword. Slander is the weapon. Rashi and Meiri name the men of Ziph who informed on David (1 Sam 23:19-20) and Ibn Ezra says 'those who speak evil to Saul on his account'.

'Lie down' (eshkevah) is the ordinary word for sleeping, with a cohortative ending: 'let me lie, I will lie', calm or desperate according to the actor. KJV's 'set on fire' for lohatim makes them victims; the Hebrew participle is active, 'flaming ones', devouring (lahat is a flame, as in Psalm 104:4). And 'lions' is levaim, the poetic plural of lavi. Hebrew places 'soul' first for emphasis: it is his life, not only his body, that is in the den.

A note on grammar: the line breaks the usual order, and Ibn Ezra reads 'among' as understood before 'blazing ones'.

philological_notes.note: Active participle, 'flaming, burning ones'; the same root gives the flaming sword in Gen 3:24. Ibn Ezra reads it as if written 'among the blazing ones'.
A poetic plural of lavi, 'lion'; Metzudat Zion lists it among the names of the lion.
'their tongue a sharp sword'; the image of the tongue as a blade recurs in Psalm 64:4 and Proverbs 12:18.

verses.translation_literal: Be exalted above the heavens, O God; over all the earth, your glory.
verses.translation_dramatic: Rise, God, above the heavens. Let your glory stand over the whole earth.
verses.directors_commentary:
The camera lifts out of the den in one beat. The imperative 'ruma' is 'rise, be high', and the sentence has no verb in its second half: 'over all the earth, your glory', the verb carried over from the first line, the way a shout carries. KJV's 'let thy glory be above' adds a jussive that is only implied. Notice the gears of the psalm: down among the lions in verse 5, now straight to the highest point in the universe, and the refrain will come back in verse 12 as the frame.

Rashi's reading is gentle: God, withdraw from the lower beings, who are not worthy of your presence among them; Radak takes it as a rhetorical figure, as though until now God had not been high enough to save. A modern ear should hear the plain sense: only a God above the heavens is out of reach of those who hunt David.

philological_notes.note: Imperative of rum, 'be high, be lifted'; a prayer for God to show his height by acting.
'your glory', from kavad, 'heavy', hence weight, honour; used of God's visible splendour. This word returns as David's own 'glory' in verse 9.

verses.translation_literal: A net they prepared for my steps; it bowed down my soul. They dug before me a pit; they have fallen into the midst of it. Selah.
verses.translation_dramatic: They laid a net where my feet would fall; it bent my spirit low. They dug a pit across my path, and fell, themselves, into its midst. Selah.
verses.directors_commentary:
The hunter's kit: a net on the ground to catch the foot, a pit dug on the path, covered and baited. The hunted man, in his own image, is the game. The Hebrew repeats the shape: 'prepared ... net', 'dug ... pit', each a short clause, then the third drops the perfect into reverse: the diggers are the ones who 'have fallen'. KJV adds 'themselves' and 'whereof', which the Hebrew leaves out; the stark 'they have fallen into the midst of it' is the stage direction.

The tenses matter. Radak, Rashi and Metzudat Zion say the perfect 'nafelu' is a prophetic past: they will fall. Malbim reads it literally: the pit was already waiting when Saul walked into the cave and fell into David's hands. Either reading lets the actor play certainty. Ibn Ezra and Radak also note 'shichah' for the usual 'shuchah', a pit; Radak says the hiriq form means the same as the deep shuchah.

The subject of 'bowed down' is open: the net bent his soul, or each enemy did (Ibn Ezra), or, as KJV and ASV take it, his soul is bowed with the dread of it.

philological_notes.note: 'pit'; the form is irregular for shuchah (Psalm 119:85), and Radak says the hiriq form has the same meaning as the shuruk form 'deep pit'.
'to bend, bow down'; the unnamed subject (net, enemy or the soul itself) is a real ambiguity in the Hebrew. Rashi quotes Psalm 145:14, 'who raises all who are bowed down'.

verses.translation_literal: Steadfast is my heart, O God; steadfast is my heart. I will sing, and I will make music.
verses.translation_dramatic: My heart is steady, God. My heart is steady. I will sing, and I will make music.
verses.directors_commentary:
The turning point of the psalm, and the shift is in the verbs: from running and hiding to standing firm. 'Steadfast' (nakhon) is from kun, to be set firm, as a foundation or a tent peg; it is not a feeling of calm, it is a heart set in place. KJV's 'fixed' gets it, and YLT's 'prepared' hears the other sense of the root, readiness. The repetition is the same device as the 'be gracious' of verse 2, but now the repeat is confidence, not fear. Play it twice, the second time quieter and surer.

Then two verbs of music: 'ashirah' (sing) and 'azamerah' (make music with strings, as on a lyre). KJV's 'give praise' for the second drops the instrument. Malbim's staging is that this is the moment in the cave when David holds back from striking Saul; Rashi quotes the Jerusalem Talmud, 'steadfast with you in the measure of judgment and in the measure of mercy'.

philological_notes.note: Niphal participle of kun: 'set firm, established, ready'. Both 'fixed' (KJV) and 'prepared' (YLT) are in range.
'I will make music', the piel of zamar, which names singing to an instrument; the pair with shir 'sing' is a standard parallelism.

verses.translation_literal: Awake, my glory! Awake, harp and lyre! I will awaken the dawn.
verses.translation_dramatic: Wake, my glory. Wake, harp and lyre. I will wake the dawn itself.
verses.directors_commentary:
He speaks to his own soul, to the instruments, and to the sun, and orders all three up. 'My glory' (kevodi) is not vanity: Meiri and Metzudat Zion identify it as the soul, 'the glory of the body', and in the earlier line the word was God's; man's glory answers it. 'Nevel' and 'kinnor' are the large harp (or lyre) and the smaller lyre, the two stringed instruments of the Levites. KJV's 'psaltery' is the Greek-derived name for the first one.

The lovely turn is the last clause. Hebrew uses the causative 'a'irah', 'I will wake', with 'dawn' as the object, so David wakes the dawn and not the reverse; KJV's 'I myself will awake early' hides the audacity. Rashi, quoting the Talmud (Berakhot 3b), says other kings are woken by the dawn, but I wake it. For the actor: a man who has been hiding in the dark decides to sing the sun up.

philological_notes.note: A causative with the dawn as its object, 'I will awaken the dawn'; Ibn Ezra reads the verb as intransitive 'awake at dawn', and Meiri notes the Jerusalem Talmud makes it transitive.
'My glory', in the sense of 'my soul' (Meiri, Metzudat Zion); by the parallelism with the instruments, it may also mean the tongue or voice.

verses.translation_literal: I will give thanks to you among the peoples, O Lord; I will sing to you among the nations.
verses.translation_dramatic: I will give you thanks among the peoples, Lord; I will make music for you among the nations.
verses.directors_commentary:
The cave suddenly opens onto the world. Two parallel lines, 'peoples' and 'nations', with two verbs, 'give thanks' (hodah) and 'make music' (zimmer). Hodah is thanks as public confession: the rescued man proclaims what was done, as a witness would. Malbim distinguishes the two verbs: hodah is thanks for a good deed, zimmer is telling God's praises.

Who are the 'peoples' and 'nations'? KJV's singular 'people' flattens the Hebrew plural. Radak reads the pair as one idea said twice, both words naming the families of Israel. Ibn Ezra splits them: 'peoples' are the many of Israel (he cites 'after you, Benjamin, among your peoples'), 'nations' are those not of Israel. Malbim takes the nations as those who have a religion, to whom David will tell the LORD's praise. Either way, an actor should not play it small: a fugitive in hiding vows a stage as wide as a crowd.

The divine name changes: here 'Adonai', 'my Lord', not 'Elohim', as the psalm moves from the crisis to the public.

philological_notes.note: Hiphil of yadah, 'give thanks, confess'; in the psalms it is thanks said aloud before others.

'Peoples' and 'nations'. Radak takes both as the families of Israel; Ibn Ezra takes 'peoples' as the many of Israel and 'nations' as those not of Israel; Malbim takes them as nations that have a religion. Meiri notes that the bet of baleummim stands for lamed and should have carried a dagesh.

token_glosses.gloss: I will give thanks to you
I will sing praises to you

verses.translation_literal: For great to the heavens is your covenant loyalty, and to the skies your faithfulness.
verses.translation_dramatic: For your love is great enough to reach the heavens, and your faithfulness up to the clouds.
verses.directors_commentary:
The reason behind the vow, and the same pair as in verse 4: chesed and emet. The earlier verse had them sent down; here they stand as tall as the sky. 'To the heavens' and 'to the skies' (shechakim) are both measures of height: shechakim is the thin upper air, the dust of the clouds, the thinnest edge of the visible. KJV's 'mercy' and 'truth' is sound but a little soft; ASV's 'lovingkindness' is closer to the covenantal sense. The Hebrew phrase is 'great unto the heavens', with no verb, 'great' being the whole claim.

Ibn Ezra ties it to the line before: because the enemy reproached, God will send his loyalty, for it is great to the heavens. Malbim notes that Psalm 36:6 says the same about God's chesed in the heavens and his faithfulness unto the skies, and that here it answers the 'Most High' of verse 3. A good actor will play it as an answer to the opening cry: the heaven David asked for help from is itself full of the thing he needs.

philological_notes.note: 'Skies, clouds', from the root of 'fine dust, thin': the upper air. In Psalm 36:6 it forms the same pair with 'heavens' and 'faithfulness'.

verses.translation_literal: Be exalted above the heavens, O God; over all the earth, your glory.
verses.translation_dramatic: Rise, God, above the heavens. Let your glory stand over the whole earth.
verses.directors_commentary:
The refrain returns word for word, with one small change: verse 6 says 'above the heavens' with the article (ha-shamayim), and verse 12 says 'above heavens' with none. Radak says it is repeated to strengthen the plea, and that is how to play it: the same words as verse 6, but now from a man who has seen the dawn, no longer from the den. The cry that was a plea in verse 6 is a closing hymn here, the last phrase of a song that began with a man in a cave.

KJV hardly differs between the two verses (it only changes a semicolon to a colon), so the refrain is audible in English only if the speaker gives it a different weight the second time. Metzudat David takes it as the result: through the great rescue, God's glory is raised above heaven and earth.

philological_notes.note: The refrain of verse 6, here without the article before 'heavens'; the psalm closes as it was about to close the first half.
